title: Chapter 77 – The Cradle Answers
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Feng finds him at the Pill Hall wall at dusk and says it without preamble.

"They are going to seal the fortieth landing."

Jian looks up from the stone mortar. His brother stands in the arch of the herb-store gate with his hands behind him and his weight on his good leg. The sky behind him is the color of dishwater. Snow has not yet fallen, but it is in the air; the cold has the thin clean edge of it.

"When?"

"Day after tomorrow. Elder Duan has ordered an inspection of the post. Keeper Fu told him the array read forty-two on a boy who did not move." Feng's voice is dry and low. "Duan said that an array which cannot count is an array that has been tampered with. He intends to take the post apart. Stone by stone, if needed. The landing is closed to everyone from the second bell."

Three days. No, two.

"Has he named me?"

"He named no one. He does not need to. Fu's tablet has thirty-eight on it, and Fu's other book, which Duan has asked to read, has something else." Feng's jaw is tight. "The keepers are sworn to the Hall of Enforcement. He will read it, and by tomorrow noon he will know who stood on the landing."

"Then he knows already."

"He suspects. Suspicion and knowledge are not far apart in his mouth." Feng meets his eyes. "I am on night duty on the stair tonight. Third watch. The first-ranker stands at the thirty-ninth landing and sees that no one goes up. It is a rule older than I am."

Jian says nothing.

"I have never in my life," says Feng, "been anywhere I was not supposed to be. I have been told that I will turn my back for a quarter of an hour at the third watch. I do not know why. I have not been told. I only know it is something my brother wants, and that it will not be there after tomorrow." He steps back. "Say it is a pill."

"Feng..."

"I have said it three times. I will say it a fourth." The gate creaks as he turns. "Do not make me regret it."

* * *

He weighs it for the length of the afternoon, bent over a bench of herbs he cannot see.

The costs are not a secret. He has had them in the back of his mind since the night he took the cradle from Ke Tian's belt, and the panel in the herb store has set them down plainly. He sits with the pestle going in his hand and reads them one by one, as an engineer reads a risk register.

One. Irreversibility. The cradle, once docked and integrated, cannot be removed. It becomes a part of the Interface. Whatever the Interface does after that, it does with the cradle in its bones. If the cradle is a snare, he will carry it for the rest of his life. If it is a trap set six hundred years ago by a man who wanted a child to open a door, he will have opened the door for him.

Two. Reboot. The panel has said it in so many words. The Interface will go dark. He will lose the seven points of energy he has, which are not many. He will lose his Level 3, and with it Scan, Fabrication, Synthesis. For how long, the panel has not said. He has an estimate from the one thing he understands about the system: the way it does everything on a count of days. Thirty, he guesses.

Three. Exposure. He will be on the fortieth landing, at the third watch, with a lock that hums. Whatever happens there will be heard, if not by ears, then by the keepers' arrays, the Hall's seams, a hundred things he cannot see. And he will be doing it without the Interface to warn him.

Four. Time. Thirty days without the Interface is thirty days of the reagent hunt delayed. Tan Ruyan will take the root and the boar. Mo Lian will move. The Pill Hall's trial month will end. He will have to stand in front of Elder Bai and be an apprentice with nothing but his hands.

He puts down the pestle.

And against all that.

He turns to the other column. It is shorter, and every line in it is a question.

The cradle answered the lock. Twice. Not once. He does not think that was an accident.

Heng says it is older than the Sect. A dying man with a thread in his throat, with every reason to lie. And yet the Founder's four lines on silk have the sound of a thing that is true: I have built it to be opened once more, by one like him. Let the Sect be worthy, and let it wait.

A man built that. Six hundred years ago. For me.

It is not a thought he can say aloud, or to anyone. It does not make him feel chosen. It makes him feel what he felt in the lab on the night before the first live run, years ago, in another life: the cool, grave, sickening knowledge that a thing has been designed, and that he is the part that goes in the slot.

I could refuse.

He could. He could walk away tonight and let Duan break the post. The cradle would stay in his pouch. The Interface would run as it has run. He would hunt reagents with a hundred and forty-three points of cultivation energy to earn, which he does not know how to earn, and the lock would be taken apart by men who would find nothing, and the door, if there is a door, would stay shut for another six hundred years.

Or the Sect would find what is behind it, and use it.

That is the thing that decides him, in the end. Not hope. Not trust. The plain unpleasant arithmetic of what happens if he does nothing. A thing like that, built into the heart of a mountain by the Founder himself, will not stay a secret once the Hall of Enforcement starts pulling up stones. Someone will open it. Someone who is not a child. Someone who has no idea what he is looking for.

And I will not even know what I have lost.

He sets the pestle down in the mortar. He wipes his palms on his tunic. Across the yard a furnace pops, and the smell of boiled bark rolls over him, warm and bitter.

Tonight.

Before he leaves, he does the last of his ledger.

He sits on his cot in the dark with the bark strip on his knee and the charcoal in his fingers, and writes the day's figures: eleven and a half stones earned, ten sent, one kept. Eighty points. A trial month with twenty-two days left. He writes the debt to Heng at the bottom, in a mark that nobody else would read. One. Asked once.

Then, under it, in the same small hand, he writes a line he has never written before.

If I do not come back, the bag goes to Feng. Pebble must be fed on fruit at dusk. He will not eat the dry kind.

He looks at it for a while. It is a foolish thing to have written. He tears the strip off at the line and puts it under Lan Tong's pillow, where the silent boy will find it in the morning and, with luck, not understand it.

I am not going to die tonight.

But a sensible man leaves a note, he thinks. He has left notes before, in a world with different locks.

Lan Tong's eyes are open in the dark. They follow him to the door. They do not close until he has gone.

* * *

The snow begins at the second watch.

It falls out of a sky he cannot see, fine and dry and perfectly silent, powdering the courtyard and the pines and the roofs. The Court sleeps under it. A watchman's lantern swings, far below, and goes out.

Jian leaves Reed Courtyard by the back wall.

He goes alone. He takes Mu's blade in its plain sheath, six pins in his sleeve, the small gray pouch at his hip, and the lamp he does not light. At his belt, in the beast bag, Pebble sleeps on. He wears no cloak. He wears the gray tunic and the cloth leggings and a pair of felt wraps over his sandals, and under it all, hard against his breastbone, the little cold weight of the oiled cloth.

He moves the way Hu taught him, in the forge, in what seems another life: low, quiet, with the weight in the heel. The Veil is up. He lets the false wheel turn and the true one run beneath it. Across the yard, a servant coughs in his sleep. A cat bolts under a bench. He goes through the shadow of the Pill Hall, around the Contribution Hall's flank, and out onto the stair.

It is a ribbon of white. The snow has laid a skin on every step. The jade posts at the landings stand up out of it like candles. Above, the mountain climbs into the dark and the cloud, and the stair climbs with it, and there is no sound anywhere but the faint hiss of falling flakes.

He climbs.

There is no pressure. The array sleeps, as it does between trials, and the stone is quiet beneath his feet. He had not expected the silence. It is the silence of a great machine that has been switched off. He counts the landings as they pass: ten, twenty, thirty. Cold stings his face. His breath goes up in small white clouds.

At the thirty-ninth landing, a lantern burns.

Feng stands beside the post in his gray cloak with a spear grounded at his side. He is looking out over the parapet at the sleeping Court, with his back to the stair. His shoulders are straight. The snow is gathering on them. He does not turn his head as Jian passes.

"I have not seen anything," he says to the dark.

"Thank you."

"I will see nothing for a quarter of an hour." A pause, and then, lower, in a voice Jian has not heard since the Garden: "Come back down."

Jian does not answer. It is not a promise he can make.

He goes up the last flight alone.

* * *

The fortieth landing is white and silent and entirely empty.

The snow lies a hand deep on the paving. The four corner posts stand like sentinels. In the center the tall post rises with its white disk, and the disk is dark, and he does not think it is asleep.

He crosses the snow. His felt wraps squeak faintly. He stops two paces from the post and kneels, and puts his left hand flat on the paving, and with the other hand brushes the snow from the stone in a wide circle.

It is the same stone as it was at dawn. Polished gray. Cold. Beneath his palm, he feels nothing at all.

Seam-sight.

He looks for it with the inner eye. It is there, as it has been all day, a faint cold pulse in the dark behind his eyes, the Level 3 passive, the quiet gift that has cost him nothing and failed him never. The world comes apart along its joints. Beneath the polished stone, the lattice spirals inward, ring on ring, to the heart of the post. At the center, set into its cavity, the seven-lobed plate waits.

Nothing in it moves.

He opens the pouch. He takes out the oiled cloth and unwraps it on his knee. The cradle lies in his palm, a coil of silver wire as long as his finger, wound in a tight spiral on a core of dark glass. It is cold. It is, he thinks, the oldest thing he has ever held.

It leans toward the post.

He feels it in his fingers, a soft, steady, living pull, like a magnet in the dark. He lays the cradle on the paving and the pull becomes a tug, then a hand, then an urging so strong that he has to close his fingers around it to keep it from sliding.

You want to.

"I know," he says, aloud, to no one. His voice is very small in the white silence. "I know."

He rises. He carries the coil to the post, and there, before he kneels, he sees the disk.

The disk is the last thing he notices.

He has looked at it all day and thought it a blank. Now, with the post dark and the snow settling on its crown, he sees by the seam-sight what the eye misses: the white face of the stone is worn. There is a shallow hollow in it, no deeper than a coin, in the shape of a hand. A right hand. Small. Four fingers and a thumb, spread a little, the way a child's hand spreads when it is pressed to a window.

Six hundred years of palms have been laid on this disk. Hundreds of them, thousands. Every junior who reached forty has set a hand here and felt it warm, and gone down the stair none the wiser. And every one of them has laid it a little off from the hollow, wide or high or crooked, because the hollow is too small for a grown boy. It was made for a child. It has been waiting for one.

He lifts his right hand. It is the hand that held the Garden's plate, that wore a silver print for a day and a night, that Deputy Dou measured with a ruler and sent to the Arbiter on a slip of paper. He lays it in the hollow.

It fits. Every finger. The edge of the palm sinks into the stone as a key sinks into a lock, and the disk, which has been dark, opens like an eye.

The light is white and brief. It does not rise. It sinks, down the post, along the paving, into the seam at its base, and he understands that he has been recognized.

He kneels. At its base, below the disk, where the polished stone meets the paving, there is a seam: a hair-fine line he would have missed if he had not been looking. He runs his thumb along it. A section the size of his palm gives under the pressure, with a sound like a sigh, and slides inward.

Behind it lies a hollow.

It is round. It is the exact width of the coil. At its center, a ring of seven small notches. And around its rim, for the last time, the whole fortieth landing comes quietly, perfectly, alive. Lines of pale light run out from the post across the snow like cracks across ice. The jade corner posts begin, one by one, to glow. A deep, slow, rising note fills the air, very low, and the snow on the paving shivers into a thousand drifting motes.

It is waking.

He thinks, absurdly: Feng will hear. He thinks: Duan will hear. He thinks of the Founder, six hundred years dead, who built this thing and waited, and he is no longer sure whether the fear in his chest belongs to him.

He puts the cradle into the dock.

* * *

```
CRADLE DETECTED.
Dock: authorized. Anchor: Hundred Stairs, landing 40.
Verification: SEVEN-LOBE KEY ... MATCH.
Verification: HOST (right palm) ... MATCH.
Verification: PRIOR HOST ... not found.

ARK-7 INTERFACE — INTEGRATION PROTOCOL
This action is IRREVERSIBLE.
Effects of integration:
- Interface status: REBOOT REQUIRED.
- Cultivation Energy (CE): 7 -> 0.
- Interface Level: 3 -> 1, for 30 days.
- Scan, Fabrication, Synthesis: DISABLED for 30 days.
- Stored knowledge, recipes, memories: RETAINED.
- Seam-sight (passive): DISABLED for 30 days.
- Cradle: permanent.
Benefit (on restart): synthesis ceiling will rise. Further benefits: not disclosed.
Restart condition: Moon-ash ritual. Not available before day 30.

PROCEED? [Y / N]
```

He reads it three times. The panel is cold and clean and exact. There is no flourish in it, and no warmth. It lists the costs as the Interface has always listed them, in order, without comment. He has the strange impression that the system has been waiting a long time for the question.

Thirty days.

Restart condition. Moon-ash ritual.

It is a thing he does not know. He has never heard of it. In his head, a drawer opens and is empty. He holds the line in his mind and marks it, as he marks everything he does not understand, for later.

His knees are numb in the snow. The note in the air has deepened. Somewhere far below, a bell strikes the half hour, and the sound is thin and strange, as if heard through water.

Yes.

It is not a leap. It is a step, taken with the full weight of what is on the other side. He has done the sums. He has priced the cost. He has chosen the narrow road because the wide one ends in a room full of strangers with crowbars.

Y.

The panel flickers.

* * *

It does not hurt at first.

The cradle trembles in its socket. A thread of silver runs out of it, thin as a hair, across the paving, and touches his knee. Then another. Then a dozen, a score, a hundred, a web of living light that spreads from the dock across the snow in the shape of a hand with seven fingers. They climb his legs. They run up his arms. They find his palms, the right, the left, and sink in without a sound.

He feels them go under the skin.

Then the pain comes.

It is not the pain of a wound. It is the pain of a thing being rearranged. A line of white fire runs up his right arm from the wrist to the shoulder, across his chest, up the back of his neck. His teeth lock. His spine arches. He is aware, distantly, that he is on his knees in the snow with his mouth open, and that no sound is coming out, and that his heart has stopped, or has begun to beat in a different rhythm.

Don't scream. Feng.

The silver web pulls tight. He feels the Interface open in his head like a wound. It is a place he has always known and never seen: a vast pale quiet, a clean white room, a library without walls. He has stood in it a hundred times, at the edge of sleep, and never looked down. He looks down now. The floor is not a floor. It is a plain of light, laid out in squares, each square a function, a line of command, a rule. He sees the Scan. He sees the Fabrication, the Separation, the Synthesis, the whole architecture of the thing he has used for ten months and never once understood.

He sees, for one instant, something that is not a square.

It is a room. A long low room under white light, with a bench running down the middle of it, black and flat and scored with fine lines, and a lid of gray metal lifted on its hinge. A hand rests on the lid. It is his own hand, the hand he had before, long and pale and ink-stained, and the sleeve above it is white. On the underside of the lid, stamped in small square letters, a code.

ARK-6.

There is no sound. There is no one there. But he knows, as one knows a stair in the dark, that this is not a memory of his own. It belongs to the place he is standing in. It is an old picture, kept in the white room for a long time, and the cradle has just knocked it loose.

It is gone before he can read the rest.

Then he sees, in the corner, something that has just closed.

It is a square in the shape of a coil. It slides into its slot with a small clean click. And the whole white room goes dark.

* * *

He comes back to the sound of snow.

It is still falling. It is falling on his face. His lashes are crusted with it, and his hands are lying open on the paving, and the fortieth landing is dark again, the posts dull, the disk dull, the lines of light gone. The hollow at the base of the post is closed. There is no seam. There is no cradle.

He has not moved. It cannot have been long. Below, the bell of the half hour is still ringing its last thin note.

Seam-sight.

Nothing. The world does not come apart. It is a stone, a post, a field of snow. There is no lattice beneath it, no spiral, no plate. It is only a landing, very quiet, and cold.

I cannot see.

He had known it. He had read the line. But it is a different thing to reach for a sense that has been part of him for months and find a smooth blank wall. His hands begin to shake, and he presses them hard against his thighs until they stop.

In the bag at his belt, something stirs.

It is faint and small and furious. A hot prickle runs along his hip. The cloth of the bag trembles, once, twice, as if a creature inside were turning over in its sleep and had been startled by a dream. A wash of feeling comes through the bond: not words, never words, but a rush of cold, a flash of fear, the sensation of falling down a long dark stair. It lasts the space of a breath.

Pebble.

"It's all right," says Jian, aloud, hoarsely. "It's all right. I'm here."

The trembling stops. He lays his palm over the bag and holds it there, the way he would hold a hand against a sleeping child's back, and sends down the bond the only thing he has: the slow steady rhythm of his own breath. In, and out. In, and out. It is not much. It has worked before. The feeling fades to a drowsy dull warmth. The small hard shape in the bag turns once and is still, and is asleep again, with the vague grudging contentment of a creature who has decided that whatever it was, it can be dealt with in the morning.

He lets his breath out in a long white plume. Below him, on the thirty-ninth landing, a spear butt knocks twice against stone: Feng's signal, the quarter hour nearly done. Jian does not answer it yet.

Alive. Intact. Still me. He counts his fingers, one hand and then the other, the way he did on the first morning in this body, and each finger is where it should be, and the count comes out right.

He stays on his knees in the snow for a little longer. He is afraid to stand. In his head there is nothing: no panel, no glow, no faint dry count of cultivation energy in the corner of his sight. It is the oldest silence he has ever heard. He had not known how much of his thinking had been done in the presence of the thing. He had not known that a mind can be accompanied.

Thirty days.

And then, thin and distant and cold, at the very edge of his sight, a line of text.

It is not white. It is a pale, dull, steady gray, like the first light before dawn. It does not flicker. It is set in the corner of his vision, exactly where the old panel always sat, and it has no border.

```
Booting.
Fragment 3 not found.
Searching.
```
